newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Gov. signs far-reaching welfare reform law.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Gov. signs far-reaching welfare reform law.

text.p: California Governor Pete Wilson signed a far-reaching welfare reform law on Monday that sets time limits on how long people may receive aid and aims to move recipients from welfare to work.
Wilson said the new law would free "hundreds of thousands of men, women and children from a system of dependency that for too long has destroyed their hopes and stifled their ambition."
"From now on, welfare in California will be a temporary transition and it will be strictly time-limited," the Republican governor said in a statement.

Wilson's office said the welfare reform bill, called the California Work Opportunity and Responsibility to Kids (CalWorks) plan, would "replace the state's failed welfare system with new rules based on work, accountability and personal responsibility."
The new law has been criticised by some Democrats who say it is too harsh on the poor.
The new law contains a cumulative lifetime limit on aid of five years, including aid received from any other state before a recipient's move to California.

New applicants are eligible to receive assistance for 18 months at any one time, while current recipients are eligible for 24 months. Counties have the option of extending the 18-month deadline for up to six months.
If the recipient has not found a job when the time limit is reached, he or she enters community service employment.

Single parents must participate in work for at least 20 hours each week beginning January 1, 1998, 26 hours each week beginning July 1, 1998 and 32 hours each week after July 1, 1999, according to Wilson's office.

The welfare reform plan, passed by the legislature earlier this month, was hammered out in tough negotiations between Wilson and Democratic legislative leaders. Disagreement on welfare was a key stumbling block to passage of the state budget, which was finally approved by the California legislature on Monday.
